title: Why Balance Matters
summary: Picking up exactly where Data Structures I left off: a plain BST degrades to O(n) on a lopsided tree, and this discipline exists to fix that guarantee for good.

title: AVL Trees: The Balance Invariant
summary: A binary search tree that enforces one simple rule after every insertion or deletion — the heights of any node's two subtrees never differ by more than one.

title: AVL Rotations: Single and Double
summary: The local, constant-time restructuring operation — a rotation — that restores AVL's balance invariant after an insertion or deletion knocks it out of alignment.

title: Red-Black Trees: An Alternative Balance Scheme
summary: A looser balance invariant, enforced with a color on every node instead of a strict height check — the scheme most production libraries (Java's TreeMap, C++'s std::map) actually use.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Algorithms and Complexity Knowledge Area

title: Comparing AVL and Red-Black Trees in Practice
summary: Both guarantee O(log n) operations — the real difference is in the constants: AVL's stricter balance means faster lookups but more rotations; red-black's looser balance means the reverse.

title: The Heap Property
summary: A binary tree where every node is at least as large as (or at least as small as) both of its children — weaker than a BST's ordering, but exactly enough to make "find the max" instant.

title: Array Representation of a Binary Heap
summary: Storing a complete binary tree in a plain array — a node at index i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 — avoiding pointers entirely and packing the tree with zero wasted space.

title: Heapify: Building a Heap in Linear Time
summary: Turning an arbitrary array into a valid heap in O(n) time, not the O(n log n) a naive one-at-a-time insertion would cost — a genuinely surprising result worth deriving carefully.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Algorithms and Complexity Knowledge Area

title: Heap Insert and Extract-Max/Min
summary: The two operations a priority queue actually needs — adding an element and removing the highest (or lowest) priority one — each done in O(log n) by bubbling along a single root-to-leaf path.

title: Heapsort
summary: Heapify the whole array once, then repeatedly extract the max into the back of the array — an O(n log n), in-place sort that falls directly out of the heap operations already covered.

title: The Union-Find (Disjoint-Set) ADT
summary: A structure for tracking a collection of disjoint groups, supporting exactly two operations — merge two groups, and ask whether two elements are in the same one.

title: Quick-Find and Quick-Union
summary: Two naive first attempts at implementing union-find — one makes membership-checking instant but merging slow, the other the reverse — neither good enough on its own.

title: Union by Rank and Size
summary: The first key optimization: always attach the smaller (or shallower) tree under the bigger one's root, which alone caps every tree's height at O(log n).

title: Path Compression
summary: The second key optimization: while walking up to find a group's root, point every node visited along the way directly at that root, flattening the tree for every future lookup.

title: Amortized Analysis of Union-Find
summary: Combined, union by rank and path compression make a sequence of operations run in almost — but not quite exactly — constant time each, a famous result involving the inverse Ackermann function.

title: Tries: Prefix Trees for String Keys
summary: A tree where a key's characters are spelled out one per edge along a root-to-node path — keys sharing a prefix share that prefix's path, something no hash table can offer.

title: Trie Operations: Insert, Search, Prefix-Match
summary: Inserting and searching a trie one character at a time, and the operation a hash table fundamentally cannot do efficiently — listing every key that starts with a given prefix.

title: Ternary Search Tries
summary: A space-efficient trie variant using three children per node instead of one per alphabet character, trading a little search speed for a dramatically smaller memory footprint.

title: Real Applications: Autocomplete and Routing Tables
summary: Two genuine, well-known uses of prefix trees — a search box's autocomplete suggestions, and a router's longest-prefix-match lookup for forwarding IP packets.

title: Choosing a Data Structure: A Decision Guide
summary: A side-by-side decision guide across every structure covered in Data Structures I and II — hash table, BST, AVL/red-black tree, heap, union-find, trie — organized by what each one is actually good at.
